s: Cheshire's biggest house, held by one family for 600 years
w: Granted to Sir Thomas d'Anyers in 1346 and held by the Legh family from 1388 until given to the National Trust in 1946, Lyme is the largest house in Cheshire - part Elizabethan, part 1720s rework by Giacomo Leoni blending Palladian and Baroque. Its library holds the Lyme Caxton Missal, an early book printed in England.
_facts: Estate granted to Sir Thomas d'Anyers in 1346, passed to the Leghs of Lyme by marriage in 1388
Held by the Legh family until given to the National Trust in 1946
Remodelled in the 1720s by Giacomo Leoni, mixing Palladian and Baroque styles
Library holds the Lyme Caxton Missal, an early book printed by William Caxton

s: A Norman lord's castle that hosted a Scottish king
w: Founded by William Peverel after the Conquest, this ruin anchored the Honour of Peverel and hosted Henry II three times, including a visit from King Malcolm IV of Scotland. The Crown seized it in 1155, keeping it even after the Earls of Derby paid 2,000 marks for the Peak lordship. It commands the Hope Valley below.
_facts: Founded between 1066 and 1086 by William Peverel, caput of the Honour of Peverel
Confiscated by Henry II in 1155; Henry visited in 1157, 1158 and 1164, hosting Malcolm IV of Scotland
Garrison increased during the Revolt of 1173-74, shared with Bolsover and Nottingham castles
William de Ferrers, 4th Earl of Derby, paid 2,000 marks for the Peak lordship in 1199

s: A vanished castle, chased by treasure hunters for centuries
w: One of the earliest stone castles in North West England, Buckton was already a ruin by 1360, surviving only as buried foundations under heather and peat. Treasure hunters dug here in the 18th century after rumours of gold; later it served as a wartime decoy. Volunteers mapped what was left between 1996 and 2010.
_facts: Medieval enclosure castle, one of the earliest stone castles in North West England
Earliest surviving record from 1360 describes it as already derelict
18th-century rumours of buried gold and silver drew treasure hunters to the site
Used as a WWII anti-aircraft decoy; excavated 1996-2010 by the Tameside Archaeology Survey

w: A natural limestone cave two million years in the making, carved by the same underground Wye system that still runs beneath Buxton. Its age and geology have earned it Site of Special Scientific Interest status - one of the Peak District's oldest visitable spaces.
_facts: Two-million-year-old natural limestone cave on the edge of Buxton
Forms part of the River Wye's underground cave system
Designated a Site of Special Scientific Interest

s: Where five rivers rise and three counties meet
w: Five rivers - the Dove, Manifold, Dane, Wye and Goyt - all rise on this windswept gritstone moor, and three counties meet at its edge, at a spot called Three Shire Heads. It once claimed England's second-highest pub, the Cat and Fiddle Inn, closed in 2015 and later reopened as a distillery.
_facts: Major gritstone moorland southwest of Buxton, highest point 551 metres
Source of the rivers Dove, Manifold, Dane, Wye and Goyt
Derbyshire, Staffordshire and Cheshire meet at Three Shire Heads on its flank
Site of the Cat and Fiddle Inn, England's second-highest pub, closed 2015 and reopened as a distillery

s: A lead-mining dynasty's manor, remodelled for two centuries
w: Bought into the Gell family in 1553, this manor grew rich on Wirksworth lead mining and stayed in Gell hands - through a baronetcy, its extinction, and two centuries of inheritance by marriage - until the estate was broken up in the 20th century. It produced an admiral and a religious patron along the way.
_facts: 14th-century manor house associated with the Gell family baronets from 1553
Historically linked to Wirksworth lead mining
Baronetcy created 1642, extinct 1719; estate passed by marriage several times
Notable Gell descendants include Admiral John Gell and religious patron Katherine Gell

s: A Roman fort whose civilian town hid for centuries
w: Built around AD 79 above the Castleshaw valley, this fort was abandoned within two decades and replaced by a smaller fortlet - around which a civilian settlement grew, unnoticed until the 1990s. It may have been a logistical outpost before being abandoned again in the 120s, now protected as nationally important.
_facts: Roman fort (castellum) built c. AD 79, abandoned in the 90s
Replaced c. 105 by a smaller fortlet with a surrounding civilian settlement
Civilian settlement lay undiscovered until the 1990s
Protected as a scheduled monument of national importance

s: A castle whose birth date historians still argue about
w: Was it raised by Edward the Elder in 924 against the Mercians, or built later by Norman lord Ralf Gernon? Historians never settled it - 1960s digs found only 12th-century pottery, though some think a Norman motte was built over an older Saxon stronghold. Razed in the Civil War, it left only earthworks on Castle Hill.
_facts: Motte-and-bailey castle in Bakewell, Derbyshire
Some sources date it to 924, built by Edward the Elder against Mercian invasion
Others attribute it to 12th-century lord Ralf Gernon; 1969/71 excavations found 12th-13th century pottery
Razed during the English Civil War; only earthworks remain on Castle Hill

s: A Bronze Age burial stacked on a Neolithic one
w: Two burial mounds in one: a Neolithic oval barrow with a Bronze Age round barrow built directly on top of it, generations of burial compressed into a single earthwork. It stands just south-west of the Arbor Low henge, part of the same prehistoric ceremonial landscape.
_facts: Large burial mound in the Peak District, Derbyshire
Thought to be a Neolithic oval barrow with an Early Bronze Age round barrow added at one end
Located about 300 metres southwest of the Arbor Low henge

s: The house that held Mary, Queen of Scots captive
w: Bess of Hardwick began building Chatsworth in 1553, living here with her fourth husband, the Earl of Shrewsbury - later entrusted with guarding Mary, Queen of Scots, whom he lodged here from 1570. She stayed in rooms above the great hall still called the Queen of Scots rooms. Cavendish family since 1549.
_facts: Seat of the Duke of Devonshire, held by the Cavendish family since 1549
Bess of Hardwick began building the current house in 1553, finished 1560s
Her husband the Earl of Shrewsbury held custody of Mary, Queen of Scots, lodging her at Chatsworth from 1570
Rebuilt from 1687 by the 4th Earl of Devonshire, retaining the Elizabethan courtyard plan

s: The heiress whose legendary elopement never quite happened
w: Called 'the most complete and interesting house of its period,' this medieval manor grew in stages from the 11th to 17th century under the Vernon family. When heiress Dorothy Vernon wed John Manners in 1563, legend grew that the couple eloped - later spun into novels. A descendant restored the hall in the 20th century.
_facts: Medieval manor house on the River Wye near Bakewell, former seat of the Dukes of Rutland
Origins in the 11th century, additions through the 13th-17th centuries
Vernon family acquired the manor by 12th-century marriage; Dorothy Vernon married John Manners in 1563
19th-century legend holds the couple eloped; 9th Duke of Rutland restored the hall in the 20th century

s: A Y-shaped reservoir watched over by a stone circle
w: The lowest of three reservoirs in the Upper Derwent Valley, Ladybower's Y-shaped arms gather the Ashop and Derwent before flowing south. Its eastern arm is overlooked by the Hordron Edge stone circle, a prehistoric watcher over a modern piece of engineering. Fairholmes visitor centre sits at its northern tip.
_facts: Large Y-shaped reservoir, lowest of three in the Upper Derwent Valley
Fed by the River Ashop from the west and the River Derwent from the north
East arm, fed by Ladybower Brook, is overlooked by the Hordron Edge stone circle
Fairholmes visitor centre sits at its northern tip

s: Where the factory system as we know it began
w: Richard Arkwright built the world's first water-powered cotton spinning mill here in 1771, more or less inventing the factory system that reshaped Britain. Grade I listed and now the centrepiece of the Derwent Valley Mills World Heritage Site, it has been repurposed as a visitor centre with shops and cafes.
_facts: World's first water-powered cotton spinning mill, built by Richard Arkwright in 1771
Grade I listed building
Centrepiece of the Derwent Valley Mills UNESCO World Heritage Site
Now a multi-use visitor centre with shops, galleries, restaurants and cafes

s: The 'Shivering Mountain' that swallowed a road
w: Landslips down its eastern face are frequent enough to earn it the name Shivering Mountain, and in 1979 one beat the council, closing the A625 for good. A Bronze Age hillfort crowns the summit, and four show caves at its foot - including Blue John Cavern - once yielded lead and rare minerals. Hobbes called it a Wonder.
_facts: 517m hill near Castleton, nicknamed Shivering Mountain for its frequent landslips
A625 road closed permanently in 1979 due to landslip damage
Summit crowned by a late Bronze Age/early Iron Age hillfort and two bowl barrows
Four show caves at its base (Blue John Cavern, Speedwell, Peak, Treak Cliff) mined lead and Blue John

s: The bog that used to be Cheshire's highest point
w: Its bare peat plateau was once so dark and sodden it gave the hill its name - and its summit was the county top of historic Cheshire, at the tip of the old Cheshire Panhandle. Restoration work has since greened the exposed peat, and a paved Pennine Way now carries walkers across dry-shod even in the wettest weather.
_facts: Highest hill in West Yorkshire at 582 metres, third-highest summit in the Peak District
Historic county top of Cheshire, at the tip of the 'Cheshire Panhandle'
Crossed by the Pennine Way, now paved to protect the boggy peat surface
Highest point within a metropolitan county in the United Kingdom
